segments.text: At forty, everyone's arms get too short.

On <sub alias="two hundred and ninety-six">296</sub> real patients from published clinical data, Small Print's starting strength matched the clinician <sub alias="eighty-six percent">86%</sub> of the time, as often as the standard age table. <break time="250ms"/> And unlike the table, it held back reading glasses from about half of the short-sighted patients.

<sub alias="Eight hundred and twenty-six million">826 million</sub> people can't see well up close. <break time="200ms"/> Reading glasses cost about <sub alias="two dollars">$2</sub>, and in randomised trials they raised productivity by <sub alias="twenty-two percent">22%</sub> and income by a third.
Small Print turns your phone's camera into a ruler, right on the device.
Swipe the way the E points: no reading needed.
The letter E is redrawn about thirty times a second, so it always looks the same size to your eye.
If it can't see real eyes, it refuses to measure.
Then check the pair at the rack: the app measures where you see sharply through the glasses, and checks your reading distance sits in the middle.

It's built on AWS with CloudFront, Lambda, DynamoDB and Polly, for about <sub alias="sixty cents per thousand">60 cents per 1,000</sub> screenings, by a coding agent connected through the AWS MCP Server.
Small Print. <break time="300ms"/> Everyone deserves to read the small print.
